opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few reasons, and none of them are because the big labs aren't smart enough. They have incredible people. It's more about incentives and focus.

First, math is a relatively small market if you look at it narrowly. If you're a large AI company, your main priority is a general-purpose model that serves hundreds of millions of users: coding, writing, customer service, enterprise workflows. Math research, especially formal mathematics, looks like a niche. A team spending a year building infrastructure for a proof assistant like Lean doesn't obviously move the needle on revenue or user growth in the next quarter.

Second, the kind of work we do is very deep and very specialized. Doing AI for math properly isn't just training a model to get good scores on competition problems. You need people who understand formal verification, who can write and read Lean, who know the research frontier in mathematics, and who also understand reinforcement learning and large-scale training. That combination is rare. A big lab can hire a few of these people, but building a whole organization around that intersection is a different bet.

Third, there's a question of what you're optimizing for. Large labs often treat math as a benchmark, a way to show reasoning ability. For them it's a means to an end. For us, math is the end, or at least the core. We care about things like whether a proof is actually verified, whether the system can do autoformalization reliably, whether it can contribute to open problems. Those goals lead to very different engineering choices. When you're verifying with a formal system, you get a ground-truth signal that's extremely clean, and that changes how you design data pipelines, training, and evaluation.

And fourth, honestly, there's a timing and risk-tolerance aspect. Formal math has a lot of upfront cost. The libraries are incomplete, the data is scarce, and the payoff is long-term. A startup can afford to be obsessive about one direction. A big company has to balance a portfolio, and something with a long horizon and uncertain commercial return tends to get deprioritized, or it lives as a small research effort rather than the main mission.

So I see it less as "they can't" and more as "it doesn't fit their shape." And that's exactly the gap where a focused team can do something meaningful. I also believe that if you really crack mathematical reasoning with verification, it won't stay niche. It extends to verified software, chip design, anything where correctness really matters. But you have to be willing to commit to it first.

r001.rationale: The response says large labs prioritize general-purpose work such as coding and view math as niche, but it does not suggest that deploying the same talent to code generation would deepen their competitive moat.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it comes down to a few things, and honestly they're all rational from where a big lab sits.

The first is just incentives. If you're a large AI company, your revenue comes from consumer chat, from enterprise, from coding assistants. Math, in the sense we mean it, formal reasoning, verified proofs, actually contributing to research mathematics, is a tiny market by comparison. It's hard to justify a dedicated team of serious mathematicians when the same compute and headcount could go into something that moves next quarter's numbers. The big labs do care about math, but mostly as a benchmark, as a proxy for general reasoning. Once the model scores well on the competition problems, the internal pressure to go deeper mostly disappears.

The second is that the work is genuinely slow and unglamorous. Formalizing mathematics in something like Lean, building the infrastructure so a model can check its own work, collaborating with mathematicians who move on timescales of months and years rather than release cycles. That doesn't fit the cadence of a company that ships a new model every few months and needs a headline each time.

The third, and I think this is the deepest one, is a difference in belief about what matters. A lot of people at the frontier labs believe scale solves everything, so why specialize? Their bet is that a sufficiently general model will just do mathematics as a side effect. Our bet is different. We think mathematics is special, that verification changes the game, that you can get a feedback loop that doesn't depend on human labels, and that the systems which learn to reason rigorously in that setting will end up being important well beyond math. That's a contrarian position, and contrarian positions are hard to hold inside a large organization with a lot of consensus pressure.

And frankly, there's a talent angle. The people who want to do this, who are world-class mathematicians and also want to build, are rare, and they don't necessarily want to be one small team inside a giant company. They want to be somewhere the mission is the whole company. So in a way the big labs not doing it is what creates the space for us to exist.

r001.rationale: The candidate mentions coding assistants as a revenue source and says resources could go toward improving next-quarter results, but does not say that the company could use the talent to deepen its competitive moat in code generation.

astra-6.text:
I think it comes down to priorities. A large AI company might be very interested in math, but it also has to decide how much to invest in a specialized research direction versus improving a general-purpose model that serves a much broader audience.

And there’s a distinction between getting better at solving math problems and building something that helps mathematicians do research. For research, you need to explore ideas, work through failed approaches, and make progress on questions where you don’t have an answer to check against. That can require a different workflow and a longer time horizon.

So I wouldn’t assume they think it’s unimportant. It might simply be harder to justify internally compared with other opportunities. For a focused team, that same work can be the entire mission.

r001.rationale: The response discusses prioritizing general-purpose models over specialized math research, but it does not mention code generation or deepening a competitive moat as the alternative.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it comes down to priorities. A large AI company has to decide where to put its compute and its researchers, and math is competing with a lot of other things that have a more immediate commercial payoff. If you can improve a product that millions of people already use, that’s a very clear investment. Research mathematics has a longer feedback loop, and it’s harder to know in advance which approach will work.

There’s also a distinction between getting better at answering math questions and building something that can actually help discover new mathematics. Those goals overlap, but they don’t necessarily lead you to the same research decisions. So I wouldn’t say a large company couldn’t do this. It’s more that a focused team can make it the central goal and stay with it through a lot of uncertainty.

r001.rationale: The response says large companies may prioritize products with immediate commercial payoff, but it does not mention code generation or deepening a competitive moat with the same talent.
